title: Acid rain

definition.text: Acid rain is rain, snow or other precipitation that is unusually acidic, with a low pH.

facts.text: Most water has a pH between 6.5 and 8.5, while acid rain averages about 4–5; one definition sets the line at a pH below 5.
Burning fuels and smelting ores release sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which reactions in the air turn into sulfuric and nitric acid.
Today's acid rain comes mainly from human sources such as coal-fired power stations, animal farming, fertilizers, steel mills and vehicles.
Power plants produce a quarter of the nitrogen oxides and two-thirds of the sulfur dioxide in the air.
Fossil fuels and industry emit 70 Tg of sulfur a year as SO2, against 2.8 Tg from wildfires and 7–8 Tg from volcanoes.
In 1852 Robert Angus Smith first linked acid rain to air pollution, in Manchester.
Heavily affected regions include eastern Europe into Scandinavia, the eastern third of the United States and southeastern Canada.

related: Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution

definition.text: Acid deposition is the delivery of acids from the air to the ground, either washed down by precipitation (wet) or settling without it (dry).

facts.text: Wet deposition happens when rain, snow or fog carries acids down to the surface.
Dry deposition, when particles and gases stick to ground, plants or other surfaces, can make up 20 to 60% of total acid deposition.

definition.text: Acid rain harms forests, fresh waters and soils, kills plants and animals, damages buildings and affects human health.

facts.text: Lower pH and more aluminium in surface water harm fish, other aquatic animals, microbes and plants.
Below pH 5 most fish eggs will not hatch, and below pH 4 adult fish die.
Acid kills sensitive soil microbes and disables their enzymes, causing soil functions such as decomposition to collapse.
High-altitude forests are especially vulnerable because the clouds and fog around them are more acidic than rain.
Acids react with limestone and marble in buildings and statues to form gypsum, which flakes off.
Breathing pollutants linked to acid rain, such as nitrogen dioxide, can damage the respiratory tract.

title: Controlling acid rain

definition.text: Acid rain has been reduced by scrubbing sulfur from power-station exhaust, international treaties and emissions trading.

facts.text: Flue-gas desulfurization removes 95% or more of the SO2 from a typical coal-fired station's exhaust.
Under the 1979 Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution, sulfur and particle emissions fell 30-80% in Europe and 30-40% in North America since 1990.
In emissions trading, each polluter holds allowances for its emissions and can sell those it no longer needs after installing controls, giving an economic incentive to cut pollution.
The first emissions trading market was created by the US Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 to cut SO2 at the lowest cost to society.

definition.text: Brownfield land is previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may be polluted from past industrial use.

facts.text: Definitions vary by country, mainly over whether contamination must be present.
Examples include abandoned factories, ash ponds, landfills, dry cleaners and gas stations.
Typical contaminants are spilled hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides, asbestos and heavy metals such as lead.
The US is estimated to have over 500,000 brownfield sites contaminated below Superfund level.
The term was first used at a US congressional field hearing on June 28, 1992.
Industrial brownfields can be valuable ecosystems supporting rare plants, animals and invertebrates.
Redeveloping brownfields has become a key part of large urban greening projects.

definition.text: Valuing a brownfield needs specialised appraisal, because contamination changes a site's best use and value before and after cleanup.

facts.text: The value should allow for lingering stigma and possible liability to third parties.
Normal appraisal often fails, so appraisers use contingent valuation, case studies or statistical analysis.
A 2014 study of EPA cleanup grants from 2002 through 2008 found an average benefit of almost $4 million per site, with a median of $2.1 million.
Some environmental firms team up with insurers to guarantee cleanup costs.

definition.text: Many contaminated brownfields sit unused for decades because cleaning them costs more than the land would then be worth.

facts.text: Brownfields carry an environmental stigma that can delay redevelopment.
The US Superfund law has been criticised for pushing investment to greenfields through severe no-fault liability.
Redevelopment grew in the 2000s as developable land became scarcer in crowded areas.
Governments offer help: the EPA awarded nearly 1,000 cleanup grants worth almost $190 million from 2002 through 2013, and cleanup costs are fully tax-deductible.

definition.text: Brownfield remediation is cleaning contaminated former industrial land so it can be reused.

facts.text: Techniques include heating soil in place, bioremediation, in situ oxidation and soil vapour extraction, often combined.
Binders can be mixed into soil to stop chemicals leaching.
Phytoremediation uses deep-rooted plants to draw heavy metals out of the soil.
